newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi River still shut near Baton Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi River still shut near Baton Rouge.

text.p: A two-and-a-half mile section of the Mississippi River near Baton Rouge, Louisiana, remained closed early Wednesday afternoon, but officials said they would allow a few vessels to move through the area later today.

"Officially, the river is closed, but we will start moving traffic on a case-by-case basis...sometime this afternoon," said Commander Kenneth Parris of the Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in New Orleans.
A segment of the river from miles 233-235.5 has been closed to all marine traffic since late Monday, when a tow of 25 barges collided with a bridge just north of Baton Rouge.

Two paddlewheel steamboats carrying some 600 passengers that had been stranded in the wake of the accident would be the first to transit the closed river segment under Coast Guard surveillance, Parris said.

If the steamboats successfully navigate the area, other vessels may be allowed to pass through one at a time, officials said. In addition to the two tourist ships, officials said around 10 northbound and 15 southbound barge tows were backed up on the river.
"This will be a very slow process," Parris said, adding that traffic on the river would probably be heavily controlled for at least another day.
One of the damaged barges was believed have leaked a petrochemical called pyrolysis gasoline into the surrounding area and water.

Concern about potentially noxious fumes complicated clean-up efforts and prompted the evacuation of homes and a university near the river, but officials stressed that there was no longer a threat of breathing harmful vapors near the accident site.
Navigation restrictions imposed along the length of the Mississippi immediately after the accident will remain in place once salvage operations are completed, officials said.
In addition to tow-size and horsepower limits, the area north of the accident will be open for daylight transit only until April 5, they said.
Officials have yet to determine what caused the mishap, but they acknowledged that high water and swift currents produced by recent heavy rains might have been a factor.
((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
